name: Temperate deciduous / mixed forest
notes: Broadleaf deciduous forest dominated by oaks, beech, maples and ash with a hazel/spicebush shrub layer and a spring-ephemeral herb carpet; drawn on lowland Europe, the eastern USA and temperate East Asia (Japan/China).

canopy.name: American beech

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: two broad, fan-folded cotyledons, then thin, toothed, papery leaves. Seedlings and root suckers survive decades in deep shade as slender, zig-zag whips with long pointed buds and smooth grey bark, holding pale dead leaves through winter; suckers ring old trees with thickets of young beech.
growth.source: USDA Silvics of North America vol. 2 (Tubbs & Houston): germination in spring; very tolerant of shade; seed production from about 40 years, good crops every 2-3 years; root suckering common; 300-400 years

canopy.source: Fagus grandifolia, American beech: shade-tolerant climax tree of the beech-maple and mixed mesophytic forests of eastern North America, Nova Scotia to Florida; smooth blue-grey bark, straight-veined toothed leaves, beechnuts in spiny burs. Kew POWO for the name; USDA Silvics (Tubbs & Houston); Braun 1950 (beech-maple region).

bark.notes: smooth, thin, blue-grey bark like elephant skin, staying smooth on old trees

leaf.notes: elliptic leaves with 11-15 straight parallel veins each ending in a sharp tooth, long pointed tip

flower.form: round heads of male flowers on drooping stalks; paired female flowers

fruit.form: prickly burs 1.5-2.5 cm splitting into four to release two triangular beechnuts

appearance.seasonal: deciduous; golden bronze in autumn, young trees keep pale tan leaves all winter
appearance.silhouette: smooth grey trunk under a dense, wide, layered crown
appearance.refs: Wikipedia Fagus grandifolia; Flora of North America vol. 3; USFS Silvics

fruiting.source: USDA Silvics (flowers with the leaves in April-May; burs ripen September-October and split to drop 2-3 nuts; a high share of nuts empty; good crops every 2-3 years). Crop and decay estimated

canopy.name: Dawn redwood

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: 2 cotyledons, then soft, flat, bright green needles in opposite pairs along deciduous side shoots that turn rusty pink-brown and fall whole in autumn. The sapling is a narrow, very regular pyramid with one straight leader and horizontal branches right to the ground, growing about 1 m a year; the trunk soon flares and becomes fluted below the branches.
growth.source: Wikipedia Metasequoia (fast growing, >35 m and 1 m dbh by age 50 in cultivation; Longwood trees 41 m at 70 yr; wild trees 41-265+ yr; cones 1.5-2.5 cm, mature 8-9 months after pollination); first cone age estimated from cultivated trees

canopy.source: Hubei valley bottoms, one region; deciduous; the living fossil. Kew POWO.

traits.leaf_shape: needles or scale leaves, evergreen (larch deciduous)
traits.trunk: single straight trunk, whorled branches, conical crown
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

bark.notes: orange-brown to red-brown fibrous bark peeling in vertical strips; base strongly fluted and buttressed with deep hollows under the branch bases

leaf.notes: soft flat bright green needles in opposite pairs on deciduous shoots; fresh lime green in spring

flower.form: hanging tassels of small tan pollen cones

fruit.form: small round cones 1.5-2.5 cm on long stalks, green then brown

appearance.seasonal: deciduous conifer: turns apricot-orange then russet-bronze in autumn, bare in winter, lime green spring flush
appearance.silhouette: tall symmetrical narrow cone with a deeply fluted buttressed base and upswept branches; feathery, then a bare red-brown skeleton in winter
appearance.refs: Wikipedia Metasequoia glyptostroboides; Flora of China; Kew POWO

fruiting.source: Wikipedia (pollen cones 5-6 mm on long hanging spikes in early spring; seed cones globose 1.5-2.5 cm on long stalks, 16-28 scales in opposite pairs, mature 8-9 months after pollination); wind pollinated; cones open on the tree in late autumn-winter and then drop; crop estimated

canopy.name: Ginkgo

growth.juvenile_note: Hypogeal: the cotyledons stay inside the big seed; the shoot comes up with a few fan-shaped leaves that are often deeply notched into two or more lobes. Young trees are gawky, sparsely branched spires with a strong leader and a few long, widely spaced branches; the crown fills out and broadens only after several decades.
growth.source: Wikipedia (Ginkgo biloba: 20-35 m, some >40 m; specimens >1600 yr, largest estimated >3500 yr; conical crown when young, broader and irregular with age); Del Tredici (ginkgo ecology). Growth-age curve and first-seed age from horticultural records (females bear at ~20-30 yr).

canopy.source: Wild in the Tianmu and Dalou mountains of E China; the last of its line, unchanged since the dinosaurs. Fan leaves turn pure gold in one week each autumn, then drop all at once. Dioecious; wind-pollinated; fetid seeds carried by mammals. Kew POWO.

traits.native_range: Wild in the Tianmu and Dalou mountains of E China
traits.leaf_shape: simple or compound broad leaves, most deciduous in cold bands
traits.trunk: single trunk dividing into a rounded crown
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

bark.notes: grey to grey-brown, corky, deeply furrowed into irregular ridges on old trunks; pale grey smooth when young

leaf.notes: flat fan leaves with a notch, fine forking parallel veins, clustered on short spur shoots; bright fresh green

flower.form: small yellowish catkin-like pollen cones on males; tiny paired ovules on females

fruit.form: plum-like round seeds 2-3 cm, yellow-orange, fleshy and foul-smelling when they fall in autumn

appearance.seasonal: deciduous; turns pure clear gold in autumn and drops nearly all at once
appearance.silhouette: tall, gaunt, irregular; open pyramidal crown of a few big upswept limbs when young, broader and craggy with age; a column of gold in autumn
appearance.refs: Wikipedia Ginkgo biloba; Flora of China; Missouri Botanical Garden

fruiting.source: Wikipedia (dioecious, wind-pollinated in spring on short shoots; fertilisation by swimming sperm happens just before or after the seeds fall in early autumn; fleshy seeds 1.5-2 cm with a foul butyric-acid coat, shed with the leaves; kernels eaten cooked, ginkgotoxin in quantity). Counts estimated.

canopy.name: Maple
canopy.source: Acer saccharum, sugar maple, northeastern North America, mesic hardwood forest, 25-35 m, orange-red autumn — USDA Plants / Wikipedia

traits.native_range: Acer saccharum, sugar maple, northeastern North America, mesic hardwood forest, 25-35 m, orange-red autumn — USDA Plants
traits.leaf_shape: simple or compound broad leaves, most deciduous in cold bands
traits.trunk: single trunk dividing into a rounded crown
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

canopy.silhouette: dense oval crown, blazing orange in autumn

growth.juvenile_note: Germinates near 1 C in early spring, often under the snow. Epigeal: two long strap-shaped cotyledons, then a pair of small toothed leaves; later leaves take the familiar 5-lobed shape. Seedlings carpet the forest floor and saplings persist for decades in deep shade as slender whips 1-2 m tall, then shoot up ~30 cm a year when a gap opens.
growth.source: USDA Silvics of North America vol. 2 (Godman, Yawney & Tubbs, sugar maple): stratified seed germinates near 1 C, ~30 cm/yr height growth for the first 30-40 yr, height growth stops at ~140-150 yr, seldom flowers before 22 yr, lives 300-400 yr, very shade tolerant; SI 17-20 m at 50 yr

fruiting.source: USDA Silvics (Godman et al.): apetalous yellow flowers on long drooping stalks late Mar-mid May with the leaves, pollinated freely without insects (bees also visit); double samara 20-27 mm ripens in ~16 weeks and starts falling ~2 weeks later, into early winter; good crops in ~44% of years

canopy.name: Shagbark hickory

growth.juvenile_note: Hypogeal: the nut stays underground and a stout shoot comes up in spring after winter chilling. The seedling puts most of its growth into a deep taproot and may be only 30 cm tall after several years; saplings are straight whips with large compound leaves and big buds. The famous shaggy strips appear only on trunks about 30-40 years old.
growth.source: USDA Silvics of North America vol. 2 (Graney): hypogeal germination in spring; slow early height growth and a deep taproot; minimum seed-bearing age 40, optimum 60-200; good crops every 1-3 years; moderately shade tolerant; lives 250-300+ years

canopy.source: Carya ovata, shagbark hickory: the hickory of the eastern North American oak-hickory forest, Quebec to Georgia and Texas; bark in long strips curling away at the ends, five-leaflet compound leaves, sweet nuts in thick husks. Kew POWO for the name; USDA Silvics (Graney); Braun 1950 (oak-hickory region).

bark.notes: grey bark splitting into long, narrow plates loose at both ends and curving away from the trunk: the shaggiest bark of the eastern forest

leaf.notes: pinnate leaves of usually 5 (rarely 7) large, finely toothed leaflets, the end three much bigger, hairy tufts on the teeth

flower.form: long green catkins in threes; tiny female flowers at shoot tips

fruit.form: round nuts in a thick husk 3-5 cm that turns dark brown and splits to the base in four

appearance.seasonal: deciduous; rich golden yellow to brown in autumn
appearance.silhouette: tall straight trunk hung with shaggy curling bark strips, narrow crown
appearance.refs: Wikipedia Carya ovata; Flora of North America vol. 3; USFS Silvics

fruiting.source: USDA Silvics (flowers April-June after the buds open; nuts ripen September-October, the husk splitting freely to the base; good crops every 1-3 years, a big tree bearing up to several bushels). Crop and decay estimated

canopy.name: Tulip tree

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: two narrow, oblong cotyledons, then the unmistakable square-ended, four-lobed 'tulip' leaves on a straight green stem. In full light seedlings bolt from their second year and may be 3-5.5 m tall at five years: a straight, slender, grey-green whip with a narrow conical crown. Stump sprouts grow even faster, about 1.4 m a year.
growth.source: USDA Silvics of North America vol. 2 (Liriodendron tulipifera: 70-90 day stratification, epigeal; 3-5.5 m at 5 yr; site index 30 m: 15.8 m at 20 yr, 27 m at 40, 32 m at 60, 37 m at 100; flowers at 15-20 yr; 30-46 m mature, to 61 m; lives 200-250, up to 300 yr; shade-intolerant).

repro.note: beetle-pollinated: reads the ledger's beetle count, not bees

canopy.source: E North American cove forest; 35–50 m. Magnolia family; tallest eastern hardwood; tulip flowers. Kew POWO for the name; standard floras for range.

traits.leaf_shape: simple or compound broad leaves, most deciduous in cold bands

bark.notes: pale grey-brown with regular, interlacing, flat-topped ridges and deep furrows; young trees smooth grey with white streaks

leaf.notes: square-cut four-lobed leaves with a notched flat tip (tulip outline), bright green, on long petioles that flutter

flower.form: upright tulip-shaped cups 5 cm, pale yellow-green with an orange band at the base of each petal

fruit.form: upright cone-like clusters of winged tan samaras, persist through winter

appearance.seasonal: deciduous; clear bright golden yellow in autumn
appearance.silhouette: the tallest eastern hardwood: a huge straight columnar trunk clear of branches for 25 m, narrow oblong crown; a bare mast in winter with upright cone clusters
appearance.refs: Wikipedia Liriodendron tulipifera; Flora of North America; USFS Silvics

fruiting.source: USDA Silvics (solitary flowers 4-5 cm, yellow-green with an orange band, Apr-Jun, receptive 12-24 h; flies, beetles, honeybees, bumblebees; cone-like aggregate of samaras ripe Aug-Oct, shed mid-Oct to mid-March; 5-20% sound seed; large trees 29,000+ sound seeds). Crop count estimated.

canopy.name: White oak

growth.juvenile_note: Acorns germinate in autumn soon after they fall, sending down a deep taproot first; the shoot appears the next spring. Seedlings are slow, often dying back and resprouting for years under the canopy, with small, round-lobed leaves. In a gap the sapling becomes a straight whip, then a broad, rugged tree with massive horizontal limbs and pale, scaly bark.
growth.source: USDA Silvics of North America vol. 2 (Rogers): acorns mature in one season and germinate in autumn; acorn production begins about age 20, good crops irregular (every 4-10 years); intermediate shade tolerance; slow growing; commonly 300+ years, to about 600

canopy.source: Quercus alba, white oak: the dominant oak of the eastern North American oak-hickory and mixed mesophytic forests, from Maine and Quebec to Florida and Texas; 25-35 m with a broad spreading crown, ashy scaly bark, round-lobed leaves. Kew POWO for the name; USDA Silvics of North America (Rogers); Braun 1950.

bark.notes: light ashy-grey bark broken into loose scaly plates and shallow vertical ridges

leaf.notes: obovate leaves with 7-9 rounded, finger-like lobes and deep even sinuses, bright green above and whitish beneath

flower.form: hanging yellowish catkins in spring; tiny reddish female flowers

fruit.form: oblong acorns 1.5-2.5 cm in a shallow warty cup, ripe in one season

appearance.seasonal: deciduous; wine-red to purple-brown in autumn, dead leaves often held into winter
appearance.silhouette: broad massive crown on huge horizontal limbs, pale scaly trunk
appearance.refs: Wikipedia Quercus alba; Flora of North America vol. 3; USFS Silvics

fruiting.source: USDA Silvics (catkins with the new leaves in April-May; acorns 1.5-2.5 cm, maturing in one season, falling September-October and germinating at once; heavy crops irregular, every 4-10 years); sweet acorns eaten after leaching. Crop and decay estimated

canopy.name: Yulan magnolia

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal seedling with two thick oval cotyledons, then alternate obovate leaves with a short abrupt tip. Young trees are single-stemmed and upright with a narrow, open crown of stout grey twigs; furry grey flower buds appear only after several years, and the crown rounds out with age.
growth.source: PFAF (10 m, slow growing; beetle pollinated; seed ripe Sep-Nov, needs cold stratification, can take 18 months); Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder; age at first flowering and lifespan estimated (old temple trees in China are centuries old)

repro.note: beetle-pollinated: reads the ledger's beetle count, not bees

canopy.source: central China; 10–15 m. White goblets before the leaves. Kew POWO for the name; standard floras for range.

growth.juvenile_note: Hypogeal: the cotyledons stay inside the nut underground and the shoot comes up in spring after winter cold. First leaves are rounded, double-toothed and softly hairy like the adult. The seedling soon sends up extra stems from the base and from rhizomes 10-15 cm deep, building a clump of many slender stems that spreads into a colonial thicket.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Corylus americana (1-3 m thicket-former, rhizome sprouts 30-60 cm from parent, grows at 15% or even 1% light, good crops every 2-3 yr, flowers before leaves, nuts late summer-early fall); USDA NRCS plant guide (cold stratification); first-bearing age from hazel growers

fruiting.source: USDA FEIS (catkins open in spring before leaves; nuts ripe late summer-early fall in two leafy ragged bracts; eaten raw); hazel pollination biology from Oregon State EM 9074 (wind-pollinated, fertilization delayed months after pollination). Flower size is catkin length; fruit set, crop and nut decay estimated.

shrub.name: Flowering dogwood

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal seedling with two oval cotyledons, then opposite, smooth-edged leaves with veins curving to the tip. It grows slowly in the shade of oaks and hickories into a small, low-branched tree with tiers of horizontal branches turned up at the ends; mature bark breaks into small square blocks like alligator hide.
growth.source: USDA Silvics of North America vol. 2 (McLemore): seeds germinate in spring after cold stratification; seed bearing from about 6 years; very shade tolerant; a small tree to 10 m, rarely living more than 80 years

shrub.source: Cornus florida, flowering dogwood: the commonest understory tree of the eastern North American oak-hickory and mixed forests, Maine to Florida; 5-10 m, layered crown, four white bracts in spring, scarlet fruit and leaves in autumn. Grows as a large shrub to small tree in the shrub layer (USDA PLANTS: tree or shrub). Kew POWO for the name; USDA Silvics (McLemore).

bark.notes: dark grey-brown bark broken into small squarish blocks like alligator hide

leaf.notes: opposite oval leaves with wavy edges and veins curving toward the tip

flower.form: four broad white petal-like bracts 8-10 cm across round a button of tiny greenish-yellow flowers

fruit.form: clusters of glossy scarlet oval drupes 1-1.5 cm in autumn

appearance.silhouette: small flat-tiered tree glowing white in the spring understory
appearance.refs: Wikipedia Cornus florida; Flora of North America; USFS Silvics

fruiting.source: USDA Silvics (flowers March-May before or with the leaves, the heads framed by four white bracts; scarlet drupes ripen September-October and are taken quickly by birds; good crops most years). Crop and decay estimated

shrub.name: Great rhododendron

growth.juvenile_note: Seeds sprout on moss, rotting logs or bare wet soil; the seedlings are tiny and grow very slowly for years. The young plant is a thin sprig bearing whorls of long, dark green, leathery leaves at the tip of each year's shoot; it gains 15-20 cm a year in light shade and spreads by layering into dense, tangled 'laurel hell' thickets.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Rhododendron maximum (seeds can germinate as soon as shed, need light; 92-97% after 21 days; terminal growth 15-20 cm per season in lighter shade; seedlings grow best in partial shade but survive deep shade; stems may reach 100 yr; up to 12 m); first flowering estimated

shrub.source: Appalachian coves and stream banks; Rhododendron hells under hemlock. Kew POWO; standard floras.

growth.source: Wikipedia Ichang papeda (C. cavaleriei / C. ichangensis: 3-4.5 m, slow-growing, hardiest citrus after Poncirus, broad winged petiole, lemon-scented flowers, small fruit ripening yellow/orange with many large monoembryonic seeds and little bitter juice); Flora of China; timings estimated

shrub.name: Mapleleaf viburnum

growth.juvenile_note: Seeds need a warm then a cold period and often take two years to come up. The seedling is a small sprig with opposite, three-lobed, maple-like leaves. Plants spread by underground stems into loose colonies of slender, few-branched stems knee- to head-high under oaks.
growth.source: USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual (Viburnum: double dormancy, germination often in the second spring) and Flora of North America (Viburnum acerifolium: 1-2 m, colonial by rhizomes, in dry to mesic deciduous woods). Ages estimated

shrub.source: Viburnum acerifolium, mapleleaf viburnum: low colonial shrub of dry to mesic oak and mixed deciduous woods of eastern North America, Quebec to Georgia; three-lobed maple-like opposite leaves, flat cream flower clusters, purple-black fruit. Kew POWO for the name (Viburnaceae); Flora of North America.

bark.notes: thin smooth grey-brown stems with small pale lenticels

ground.name: Bottlebrush grass

growth.juvenile_note: Seeds come up in one to three weeks as a small tuft of flat, rough, bright green blades. From the second year the clump sends up stiff stems topped by a cylindrical spike of widely spreading, long-awned spikelets that look exactly like a bottle brush.
growth.source: USDA Plant Guide and Flora of North America vol. 24 (Elymus hystrix: cool-season bunchgrass 60-120 cm of rich, open woods; flowers June-July; short-lived). Timings estimated

ground.source: Elymus hystrix (syn. Hystrix patula), bottlebrush grass: cool-season bunchgrass of rich deciduous woods, wooded slopes and woodland edges of eastern North America. Kew POWO for the name; Flora of North America vol. 24.

leaf.notes: flat, rough, bright green blades 7-15 mm wide

flower.form: a bristly cylindrical spike 8-15 cm of spikelets standing out at right angles, each with long awns: a bottle brush

appearance.seasonal: leaves die back in winter; spikes stand tan into autumn
appearance.silhouette: loose clumps with bristly bottlebrush seed heads in the shade
appearance.refs: Flora of North America vol. 24 (Elymus hystrix); USDA Plant Guide

ground.name: Bracken

growth.juvenile_note: Young plants appear 6-7 weeks after spores land on burnt or disturbed bare soil: the first fronds are small, simple and lobed, becoming finely divided and adult-like after about 18 weeks. After up to 10 fronds a rhizome starts, which may grow 2 m in the first year; by year two the patch can be about 2 m across, sending up single, triangular, much-divided fronds from underground.
